zuitzerland.story: Zuitzerland is a temporary village for technologists and researchers, held at Laax, a mountain resort in Switzerland. It grew out of Zuzalu, a two-month gathering in Montenegro in 2023, and out of defensive accelerationism, a movement that wants to speed up technology that protects people from harm. Its organisers call it a testing ground for a network state, meaning an online community that hopes to gain its own land and rules, and they say Switzerland's decentralised system suits the experiment. A residency ran from 1 to 26 May 2025, with a summit on 17 to 19 May whose announced speakers included Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin. The Network State Atlas, a directory of such projects, lists it as active since 2024 and gives about 150 people per event. The organisers say they are building a permanent hub in Switzerland. No report says whether that hub exists, and the group has made no reported claim to legal independence.
zuitzerland.mechanism: A gathering held inside Switzerland stays under Swiss law. Describing it as a network state gives it no separate legal standing.
zuitzerland.why: Marker moved from the centre of Switzerland to Laax, the site named on the 2025 summit page, as the entry's own anchor note asked. The Network State Atlas dates the project to 2024; start year left at 2025, the first event with dates.

set.anchor: Laax, Switzerland, site of the 2025 residency and summit

zuzalu.story: Zuzalu was a temporary community of about 200 people at Lustica Bay, a resort on the coast of Montenegro. It was conceived by Vitalik Buterin, a co-founder of the Ethereum cryptocurrency network, and ran for about two months from 25 March 2023. Participants came from crypto, drug companies, politics and universities, and they stayed in resort hotels and rented homes. Topics included cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and the science of longer life, and the longevity group VitaDAO helped organise the science programme. Another topic was the network state, an idea from the former Coinbase executive Balaji Srinivasan in which an online community eventually buys land and seeks its own laws. Srinivasan appeared by video. The news site Decrypt reported that some compared the event to Burning Man for futurists and others to a sleepaway camp for the crypto elite. No land was taken and no new law was reported. Everyone remained under Montenegrin law and went home when the two months were over, and later projects such as Zuitzerland grew out of it.
zuzalu.mechanism: A temporary gathering can test how a community organises itself without any land or sovereignty, because it asks nothing of the host country's law.
zuzalu.stopped_by: It ended as planned after about two months
zuzalu.laws: Community rules only, with no legal status
zuzalu.challenge: No challenge, because it was a temporary gathering

100-year-starship.story: The 100 Year Starship is a project to study how people might one day travel to another star. It began in summer 2010 at DARPA, the US defense research agency, under its director David Neyland, working with Paul Eremenko. NASA's Ames research centre in California joined, and its director Pete Worden announced the project in October 2010 before the government had finished coordinating it, which caused friction. DARPA put in $1 million and NASA Ames $100,000. A workshop in January 2011 listed intellectual property, credibility and governance as immediate problems, and the first public symposium, in Orlando that year, drew over 700 people. In 2012 a group led by the Dorothy Jemison Foundation of former astronaut Mae Jemison won a $500,000 grant and took over the name and DARPA's intellectual property, which moved the project from government to private hands. That year Senator Tom Coburn listed it among the 100 most wasteful federal spending projects, citing a session on whether Jesus died for Klingons too. Symposia followed in Houston, in Graz in 2015 and in Nairobi in 2023, which is the last activity reported.
100-year-starship.mechanism: A government paid for the first study and then handed it to a private group. Under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, any ship that group launched would still need authorisation and ongoing supervision from a state.
100-year-starship.cost: $1.1 million in seed money from DARPA and NASA Ames, then a $500,000 grant in 2012

breakthrough-starshot.story: Breakthrough Starshot is a privately funded plan to send tiny uncrewed probes to the nearest stars. The investor Yuri Milner announced it in New York on 12 April 2016 with the physicist Stephen Hawking, and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg also sat on the board. About 1,000 probes of a few grams each would ride on sails up to 4 metres across. Lasers on the ground, with up to 100 gigawatts of power, would push them to 15 to 20 percent of the speed of light, so that they reached the planet Proxima Centauri b, a little over 4 light-years away, in 20 to 30 years. Initial funding was $100 million, and Milner put the final cost at $5 billion to $10 billion, with a first launch around 2036. In September 2025 Scientific American reported that the project was on hold indefinitely, and the physicist Philip Lubin estimated that about $4.5 million of the $100 million had been spent. No formal cancellation has been reported. Because the probes carry no people, the project raises no question of settlers' rights, and launch approval was never tested.
breakthrough-starshot.mechanism: A laser array of this size would stand on land inside some country, so that country's permission would be needed before anything could be launched.
breakthrough-starshot.cost: $100 million pledged, about $4.5 million spent, and an estimated $5 billion to $10 billion needed

icarus-interstellar.story: Icarus Interstellar is a volunteer nonprofit, registered in Alaska in February 2011, that studies how to send craft to other stars. It grew from Project Icarus, a five-year study of a fusion-powered starship started in September 2009 by Kelvin Long and Richard Obousy. That study built on Project Daedalus, a design from the 1970s by the British Interplanetary Society, a space advocacy group. The nonprofit's stated mission is to achieve interstellar flight before the year 2100, aiming at stars within 15 light-years or habitable planets within 22. Its projects included Hyperion, on ships for many generations, and Persephone, which studied ecosystems for a ship 20 kilometres long and 5 kilometres across, housing 50 to 500 people. A Starship Congress in Dallas in August 2013 drew nearly 200 people, and another was scheduled for September 2015 at Drexel University. No report describes its activity after 2015, and it has built no ship.
icarus-interstellar.mechanism: A nonprofit registered in the United States would need US authorisation and supervision if it ever launched anything, because Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty makes each country answerable for its private groups in space.

ost-article-viii-open-ended.story: The Outer Space Treaty is the main international agreement on space. It took effect on 10 October 1967 and had 118 member countries as of October 2025. Article VIII says that the country whose official list, or registry, includes a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it and its crew while they are in space or on another world. Article VII makes the launching country liable for damage the craft causes, and Article VI requires a country to authorise and keep supervising private space activity. Article VIII sets no distance at which this authority ends. Read literally, that means a ship leaving the solar system would carry its registering country's law with it for as long as the voyage lasts, and a person born aboard would come under that country's authority. This matters to anyone planning a ship that would take several generations to reach another star, because the children aboard would be subject to a law they never chose. The treaty also calls astronauts envoys of mankind. No court or government agency is known to have applied these articles to a voyage between stars.
ost-article-viii-open-ended.mechanism: Legal authority stays with the country that registered the spacecraft, and Article VIII gives no distance limit. This is the closest existing rule for a ship on a voyage of many generations.

project-hyperion.story: Project Hyperion studies generation ships, meaning crewed ships whose voyage to another star would last longer than a human life. The researcher Andreas Hein started it in December 2011 from WARR, a student group at the Technical University of Munich in Germany, as part of the Icarus Interstellar program. The team published a study of such ships in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 2012 and presented results at a European Space Agency workshop in 2019. In 2014 the researcher Cameron Smith used its data to estimate how large a population must be to stay genetically healthy over the trip. A design competition opened in 2024, with one report describing a journey of 250 years. Results came in July 2025. First place went to the Italian team Chrysalis, second to WFP Extreme of Poland and third to Systema Stellare Proximum of Malaysia. Core members later moved to a similar project at the Initiative for Interstellar Studies. Reports on the project do not say how such a ship would be governed or name a destination, and it remains a paper study.
project-hyperion.mechanism: Under Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, a generation ship would remain under the law of the country that registered it. Children born aboard would be bound by rules set before their birth.

l5-society-oneill.story: The L5 Society was an American group formed to promote large human settlements in space. In September 1974 the physicist Gerard O'Neill published "The Colonization of Space" in the magazine Physics Today, describing colonies at Lagrange points, places in the Earth-Moon system where gravity would hold an object steady. Keith Henson and Carolyn Meinel of Tucson, Arizona, read it and wrote to him, and in August 1975 they incorporated the society, named after the point called L5. Its first newsletter carried a letter of support from the presidential contender Morris Udall and said the long-range goal was to disband the society at a mass meeting at L5. O'Neill's book The High Frontier followed in 1977. No hardware was ever built, and critics said transport costs were far too high for individuals to pay. The society's main effect was political. In 1979 and 1980 it campaigned against the UN Moon Treaty, arguing that treating the Moon's resources as the shared property of all humanity would make space colonies impossible, and the United States never ratified that treaty. It also used a phone tree and a database of close to 10,000 members in a fight over funding for solar power satellites in 1980 and 1981. In 1987 it merged with the National Space Institute to form the National Space Society, which still operates.
l5-society-oneill.mechanism: A small advocacy group helped keep the United States out of the Moon Treaty by arguing that settlements need property rights the treaty would deny. Staying out of a treaty leaves a country free of its rules.
l5-society-oneill.stopped_by: Merged with the National Space Institute in 1987 to form the National Space Society
l5-society-oneill.challenge: Won a political campaign against US ratification of the Moon Treaty

assange-ecuador-embassy.story: Julian Assange, the co-founder of the leaks website WikiLeaks, lived for nearly seven years inside Ecuador's embassy in London, a suite of rooms on the ground floor of a block of flats on Hans Crescent. He entered on 19 June 2012 and asked for asylum, because Sweden wanted to question him over four alleged sexual offences and he had breached his bail in Britain. Ecuador granted asylum that August. British police could not simply go in, because under the Vienna Convention, the treaty on diplomatic relations, embassy premises are protected from entry without the permission of the embassy's government. Britain suggested it could use a 1987 British law, the Diplomatic and Consular Premises Act, to enter and arrest him, then withdrew the suggestion after Ecuador called this a breach of international law. Police instead guarded the building, at a reported cost of £6.5 million in the first two years. Swedish prosecutors dropped their investigation in May 2017. In April 2019 Ecuador's president Lenín Moreno accused Assange of repeatedly violating the terms of his asylum and ended it, and on 11 April British police, invited in by Ecuador, arrested him. He was held in Belmarsh prison until June 2024. On 26 June 2024, in the Northern Mariana Islands, he pleaded guilty to one US count of conspiring to obtain and publish national defence information. His sentence of five years and two months was counted as already served in Britain, and he was freed that day.
assange-ecuador-embassy.mechanism: Local police generally stay out of an embassy unless the embassy's own government invites them in. An embassy remains part of the host country's territory, so the refuge lasts only as long as the embassy's government agrees to it.
assange-ecuador-embassy.stopped_by: Ecuador ended his asylum and invited British police in
assange-ecuador-embassy.challenge: British police guarded the building, and he stayed nearly seven years until Ecuador withdrew its protection
assange-ecuador-embassy.recognition: Ecuador granted asylum, and Britain did not accept it

fort-st-angelo-order-of-malta.story: Fort St Angelo is a fortress in Birgu on Malta's Grand Harbour, part of which is used under a treaty by the Sovereign Military Order of Malta. The Order is a Catholic lay religious order that runs humanitarian work worldwide and traces its history to the Knights Hospitaller of about 1099. It has no territory of its own, yet it has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries and is treated by many as a sovereign body in international law, though some legal scholars dispute that. The knights rebuilt the fort from the 1530s and used it as their headquarters during the Great Siege of Malta in 1565. They lost the island to Napoleon's forces in 1798, and the British garrisoned the fort from 1800 to 1979. On 5 December 1998 Malta and the Order signed a treaty giving the Order use of the upper part of the fort, including the Grand Master's House and the Chapel of St Anne, so that it could carry out its humanitarian work from there. The treaty was ratified in 2001 and runs for 99 years, with an option for either side to give notice in the 50th or 75th year. Malta keeps ownership, its flag flies beside the Order's, Maltese courts generally have jurisdiction, and the Order may not grant asylum there. The arrangement is in force.
fort-st-angelo-order-of-malta.mechanism: A country can give a recognised body limited special status over a building by treaty while keeping ownership and most of its own law. Either side can end the deal under the treaty's exit clause.
fort-st-angelo-order-of-malta.laws: Maltese law with some listed privileges, under the 1998 treaty ratified by Malta in Chapter 429

add_sources.t: Sovereign Military Order of Malta, Wikipedia

guantanamo-lease.story: Guantánamo Bay is a US naval base on 117 square kilometres of land and water in southeastern Cuba, held under a lease since 1903. It began as a coaling station, where ships could refuel, and it is the oldest American naval base overseas. The rent was $2,000 a year in gold until 1934, when the United States changed it to dollars on its own, and since 1974 it has been $4,085 a year. A 1934 treaty says the lease can end only if both sides agree or the United States leaves the base. After the Cuban revolution, the government that took power in 1959 began protesting that the base had been imposed by force and is illegal under international law. Cuba has cashed only one rent cheque since then, and Fidel Castro said that one was deposited by mistake. Since 2002 the base has held a detention camp for people captured in the US war on terror. In Boumediene v. Bush in 2008 the US Supreme Court ruled that detainees there have a constitutional right to challenge their detention in court. The base still operates, and Cuba still objects.
guantanamo-lease.mechanism: A lease with no end date lets one country run land that another country still legally owns, even if the owner later objects.
guantanamo-lease.laws: US military and federal law, with detainee rights decided in Boumediene v. Bush
guantanamo-lease.challenge: Cuba has protested since 1959, and the base remains
guantanamo-lease.recognition: A lease between two countries, disputed by Cuba

hong-kong-new-territories-lease.story: The New Territories are the mainland and island part of Hong Kong, leased by Britain from China in 1898 for 99 years with no rent. Britain already held Hong Kong Island, taken in 1842 after the First Opium War, and the Kowloon Peninsula, taken in 1860 after the Second. In 1898, after China's defeat by Japan, Germany, Russia, France and Britain each pressed China for leases of coastal land, and Germany took Kiautschou Bay for 99 years that spring. Britain wanted land to defend its isolated colony, and on 9 June it signed the Second Convention of Peking, covering the area later called the New Territories, New Kowloon and 235 islands. The treaty is often described as an unequal one, meaning it was forced on a weaker state. The Kowloon Walled City was left out and stayed under China. Because the lease would end on 30 June 1997, Britain and the People's Republic of China negotiated in advance. Under their 1984 Joint Declaration all of Hong Kong, including the parts ceded permanently, passed to China on 1 July 1997, and the handover took place on that date.
hong-kong-new-territories-lease.mechanism: A lease has an end date. Here the date affected the whole colony, because Britain agreed in 1984 to return the land it held permanently along with the land it had leased.
hong-kong-new-territories-lease.stopped_by: The lease expired, and the 1984 Joint Declaration arranged the handover

nasseri-charles-de-gaulle.story: Mehran Karimi Nasseri was an Iranian man who lived in the departure lounge of Terminal 1 at Charles de Gaulle Airport near Paris from 26 August 1988 until July 2006. He said he had been expelled from Iran in 1977, a claim later investigation disputed, and that his papers were stolen on his way to Britain. Other accounts say he mailed them away himself. Britain sent him back to France because he had no passport, and at the French airport he could not prove who he was or what his status was. Belgium and France later both offered him residency, but he refused to sign the papers because they listed him as Iranian and did not use his chosen name, "Sir, Alfred Mehran". He stayed until he was taken to hospital in 2006, then lived in Paris shelters for 16 years. He returned to the airport in September 2022 and died there two months later. His story inspired the 2004 film The Terminal. He never claimed the terminal as a separate place, and French law applied there throughout.
nasseri-charles-de-gaulle.mechanism: An airport transit area is under the law of the country where it sits. Living there for years gives a person no separate legal status.
nasseri-charles-de-gaulle.stopped_by: Ill health ended his stay in 2006
nasseri-charles-de-gaulle.passports: He had no valid papers and refused those he was offered

panama-canal-zone.story: The Panama Canal Zone was a strip of 1,432 square kilometres across Panama that the United States governed from 1903 to 1979. It covered the canal and land about five miles either side of it, and left out the cities of Panama City and Colón. The United States wanted a canal so that its warships could move between oceans, and it negotiated with Colombia, which then ruled Panama. When the Colombian Senate held out for better terms in 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt's government gave covert support to rebels in Panama and protected them when they declared independence that November. The treaty signed on 18 November by Philippe Bunau-Varilla, a Frenchman acting for the new republic, let the United States build the canal, and the Isthmian Canal Convention proclaimed in 1904 gave it use and control of a zone in perpetuity, which means with no end date. The zone had its own governor, courts and police, its capital at Balboa, and US dollars as currency, and it cut Panama in two. That caused growing conflict, with rioting in 1958, 1959 and January 1964, after which Panamanian flags were allowed to fly beside American ones. Negotiations led to the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977. The zone was abolished on 1 October 1979, and the canal itself passed fully to Panama on 31 December 1999.
panama-canal-zone.mechanism: A treaty granting control forever can still be ended by a later treaty between the same two countries.
panama-canal-zone.currency: US dollar, with the Panamanian balboa tolerated
panama-canal-zone.laws: US law under a governor appointed by the United States
panama-canal-zone.recognition: A concession granted by treaty, meaning an area one state lets another run

snowden-sheremetyevo.story: Edward Snowden, an American who leaked secret documents about US surveillance, spent about a month in the transit area of Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow in 2013. On 23 June he flew to Moscow from Hong Kong. The United States had charged him under the Espionage Act of 1917 and with theft of government property, and the State Department revoked his passport. He had a seat booked on an onward flight to Cuba, which he did not take. WikiLeaks said he was heading for asylum in Ecuador, and he held an Ecuadorian emergency travel document. The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that Cuba had told Moscow not to let him fly, though the Washington Post described other accounts. President Vladimir Putin said Snowden was in the transit area, had committed no crime in Russia and was free to leave. About a month later Russia granted him asylum and he entered the country. He became a Russian citizen in 2022.
snowden-sheremetyevo.mechanism: An airport transit zone is not outside any country. Snowden was able to leave it only when Russia, the country it belonged to, granted him asylum.
snowden-sheremetyevo.recognition: Asylum and later citizenship from Russia

un-headquarters-zones.story: The United Nations runs its headquarters in New York and its offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi as international concessions, meaning areas inside a country where another body has been given some authority. Most local and national law still applies in them. The arrangement exists because delegates from every member country must be able to attend meetings. So the United States has a special visa, the C-2, which lets foreign officials who would otherwise be barred enter the country, on condition that they stay near the headquarters. Countries have made similar deals with each other. The Tomb of Suleyman Shah, grandfather of the founder of the Ottoman Empire, lies in northern Syria and was made a Turkish concession by the Treaty of Ankara in 1921. The tomb was moved in 1973 because a new reservoir would flood the site. In 2015 Turkey moved it again on its own because of the Syrian civil war. Syria called that move incompatible with the 1921 treaty, and Turkey has said it plans to return the tomb to its second site.
un-headquarters-zones.mechanism: An international body can run its own premises inside a country, but most of that country's law continues to apply there.
un-headquarters-zones.laws: Mostly the law of the host country

asgardia.story: Asgardia is a self-declared space nation run from Vienna, Austria, whose only territory has been one small satellite. The Russian engineer Igor Ashurbeyli announced it at a press conference in Paris on 12 October 2016. People could join online, and over 100,000 applied within two days and 500,000 within three weeks, though tougher checks cut the figure to about 210,000 by June 2017. A constitution passed that month, with no formal way to vote against it, and made the state a kingdom. On 12 November 2017 an Antares rocket from Virginia carried the satellite Asgardia-1, weighing 2.8 kilograms, into orbit, and Asgardia called itself the first nation with all its territory in space. Legal scholars disagreed, because US companies launched the satellite on a NASA-funded mission and it stayed under US authority. The Outer Space Treaty bars countries from claiming space and holds the launching state responsible for what it launches. Parliament met in Vienna, and Ashurbeyli was inaugurated as head of nation at the Hofburg palace on 25 June 2018 and re-elected with 93.17 percent in September 2022. The satellite burned up in the atmosphere on 12 September 2022, and no replacement has been reported. A press release from Asgardia reports a congress in Dubai on 30 October 2025 and claims over one million citizens. No state or UN body recognises it, and no one has ever lived there.
asgardia.mechanism: A satellite launched and registered through another country gives its owners no territory. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty keeps legal authority over it with the country that registered it.
asgardia.pop: Nobody has lived there; it claimed about 290,000 registered online citizens in March 2019 and over one million in November 2025
asgardia.currency: The Solar, a planned cryptocurrency named in its constitution, and the Lunar, a reserve unit
asgardia.passports: No issued passport has been verified
asgardia.laws: A constitution adopted on 18 June 2017, with a 150-seat parliament and a court under a Supreme Justice
asgardia.challenge: Never tested, because its satellite stayed under US jurisdiction
asgardia.recognition: None from any country or the UN
asgardia.cost: Undisclosed; NanoRacks said similar satellite projects cost about $700,000

aurora-station.story: Aurora Station was a proposed hotel in orbit from Orion Span, a startup in Houston, Texas, led by the former software engineer Frank Bunger. Announced in April 2018, it was to be a single module 35 feet long and 14 feet wide, about as roomy inside as a Gulfstream G550 business jet, circling 200 miles above Earth with four guests and two crew. A 12-day stay would cost $9.5 million per person, and a refundable $80,000 deposit held a place. Launch was planned for late 2021, with guests the following year. The company said its top technical staff came from NASA, but it would not say how much money it needed. It signed no launch contract and never started construction. An archived copy of its website said in March 2021 that operations had stopped and deposits had been refunded, while a later radio report gave 2022 as the year it closed. The company never claimed sovereignty, and it shut down before any regulator had to decide who would govern guests on board.
aurora-station.mechanism: The venture ran out of money before any question of licensing or legal authority came up. The law on private hotels in orbit remains untested.
aurora-station.stopped_by: The company closed itself; accounts date this to March 2021 or to 2022

bigelow-aerospace.story: Bigelow Aerospace was an American company in North Las Vegas, Nevada, that built inflatable modules for living in space. Robert Bigelow founded it in 1998 and paid for it himself. In 2000, after Congress cancelled a NASA inflatable project called TransHab, the company licensed the technology. It flew two uncrewed prototypes in orbit in 2006 and 2007 and in 2016 added an expandable module called BEAM to the International Space Station. By 2013 Bigelow had put in $250 million of his own money and said he would spend up to about $500 million. The company also sought clear rules for private stations from regulators. In 2014 the Federal Aviation Administration wrote to Bigelow saying it could use its existing authority over such missions, a position that lawyers at the group TechFreedom criticised as having no clear limits. In March 2020 Bigelow laid off all 88 staff and blamed the COVID-19 pandemic. When its engineering contract with NASA ended, NASA took ownership of BEAM, which remains in use on the station. The company was described as defunct as of January 2024.
bigelow-aerospace.mechanism: A private company's space habitat depended on US regulators and NASA contracts throughout. When the contract ended, the only module in use passed to a government agency.
bigelow-aerospace.stopped_by: The company laid off all 88 employees in March 2020
bigelow-aerospace.pop: Nobody lived on its free-flying modules; space station crews enter BEAM
bigelow-aerospace.laws: A 2014 Federal Aviation Administration letter on payload review, cited by lawyers
bigelow-aerospace.cost: $250 million of Robert Bigelow's own money by 2013, with up to about $500 million pledged

cloud-constellation-spacebelt.story: SpaceBelt was a plan by Cloud Constellation Corporation of Los Angeles to store customers' data on satellites in low Earth orbit and pass it between them, so that it never crossed the public internet or any country's land networks. This made it an orbital data haven, a place to keep information out of reach of national rules. The company's marketing said it would sidestep laws on how data moves between countries. Its president Cliff Beek pitched hosting data without wrangling over international compliance, and in 2017 the company offered it as an answer to GDPR, the European Union's data protection rules. Trade reporters pointed out that those rules protect European residents' data even when it is processed outside the EU. The company raised $5 million in 2016 and said it needed $480 million to reach orbit. In December 2018 it announced a $100 million commitment from HCH Group of Hong Kong. In November 2019 CFIUS, the US panel that reviews foreign investment, raised problems with that money because HCH is a Chinese company, and by April 2020 no replacement funding had been announced. That month the company announced a benchmark test with IBM. No launch has been reported, and no news of the project since 2020.
cloud-constellation-spacebelt.mechanism: The pitch assumed that data held in orbit escapes national law. Under the Outer Space Treaty, the launching and registering country keeps legal authority over the satellite holding the data.
cloud-constellation-spacebelt.cost: $480 million said to be needed; $5 million raised in 2016; a $100 million commitment in 2018 ran into US foreign-investment review in 2019

fcc-starlink-licensing.story: Outer space belongs to no country, yet a national telecoms regulator can set rules for what happens there. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) decides who may use radio frequencies to reach customers in the United States. In a 2018 order it allowed SpaceX to run a system of 4,425 satellites offering broadband internet around the world, under its Starlink plan. The FCC has also shown that it can punish a company for what it leaves in orbit. In 2002 Dish Network launched a satellite called EchoStar-7 into geostationary orbit, the band where a satellite appears to hang over one spot on Earth. In 2012 Dish agreed to move it 186 miles higher at the end of its life, out of the way of working satellites. In February 2022, low on fuel, it managed only about 76 miles. On 2 October 2023 the FCC announced its first fine for space debris. Dish admitted liability, paid $150,000 and accepted a compliance plan. Starlink's 2020 beta terms also made California law govern service on Earth and the Moon. A company that wants customers on the ground stays within reach of the regulator that licenses its signals.
fcc-starlink-licensing.mechanism: Because a satellite company needs a licence to use radio frequencies, one country can set rules for hardware in an orbit it cannot legally claim.
fcc-starlink-licensing.laws: The US Communications Act and FCC orbital debris rules
fcc-starlink-licensing.recognition: A national regulator working within the international radio system run by the International Telecommunication Union
fcc-starlink-licensing.cost: A $150,000 penalty against Dish Network in 2023

flags-of-convenience-space.story: A flag of convenience is a practice from shipping, where an owner registers a merchant ship in a country with light rules and flies that country's flag. Lawyers have asked whether spacecraft can do the same. Adrian Taghdiri wrote a 2013 note in the Boston University Journal of Science and Technology Law, as space tourism was starting, predicting that some countries would set loose rules to attract private space companies. He warned of environmental harm, more debris and danger to passengers. Space law limits the effect without removing it. Under the Outer Space Treaty, the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it and its crew. Any launching state, meaning a country that launches a craft or pays for its launch, stays liable for damage. So a cheap registry cannot remove the liability of the country whose soil was used. A presentation at a symposium of the UN's space law subcommittee in Vienna in 2016 set out the shipping idea and asked how it fits space objects. The closest working example involves orbital slots, the positions assigned to satellites. Wikipedia describes the business of Tonga's company Tongasat as in effect a flag of convenience for space, and later filings came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda. The practice has not been tested in any court.
flags-of-convenience-space.mechanism: Registration lets a company choose its regulator to some degree. Liability of the launching country keeps at least one responsible state attached to every spacecraft.
flags-of-convenience-space.laws: The UN Registration Convention and Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty

iss-intergovernmental-agreement.story: The International Space Station orbits Earth with people living on it and has no government of its own. A treaty signed on 29 January 1998 by the United States, Canada, Japan, Russia and the member countries of the European Space Agency divides legal authority among them. Under Article 5, each partner keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens on board. The European Space Agency describes this as treating those modules like part of the partners' territory, so European law applies inside Europe's Columbus laboratory, and national courts hear cases on liability and inventions. Article 22 covers crime. A Congressional Research Service paper explains that each country may prosecute its own citizens for what they do in any module. If misconduct endangers another country's citizen, or happens in or damages another partner's module, the suspect's country must consult the affected country. The affected country may then prosecute if the suspect's country agrees or gives no assurance that it will prosecute. A Crew Code of Conduct agreed in September 2000 sets a chain of command. The station is still in orbit under these rules, with seven people on board in early November 2026, and it is a patchwork of national laws with no single legal authority.
iss-intergovernmental-agreement.mechanism: The treaty shows that long-term living in orbit extends existing national law module by module. It creates no new self-governing territory.
iss-intergovernmental-agreement.pop: A rotating crew, with seven aboard in early November 2026
iss-intergovernmental-agreement.laws: Article 5 gives countries authority over their registered modules and citizens; Article 22 covers crime; a Crew Code of Conduct dates from September 2000
iss-intergovernmental-agreement.recognition: A treaty among the partner countries

kessler-limits.story: Kessler syndrome is a predicted chain reaction of collisions in orbit, and it places a physical limit on any plan to live or build there. In June 1978 the NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais published a paper called "Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt". They showed that if low Earth orbit became crowded enough, collisions would create debris, and that debris would cause more collisions. Kessler reached this by applying to satellite records a method developed for studying the asteroid belt. He found that 42 percent of catalogued debris came from 19 events, mainly explosions of spent rocket stages. At the time many people thought drag from the thin upper atmosphere would clear debris faster than it formed. By 2025 there were an estimated 11,800 satellites in orbit, of which 7,135 belonged to Starlink, and the chain reaction becomes likelier as the number grows. This bears on any claim to a place in orbit, because a settlement cannot fence off its surroundings and one operator's debris endangers all the others. No treaty sets a limit on debris. The US Federal Communications Commission's 2023 fine against Dish Network is an early case of one country enforcing its own debris rules.
kessler-limits.mechanism: Debris crosses every orbit, so activity there cannot be physically separated. That limits how exclusive any claim to a place in orbit can be.
kessler-limits.laws: No treaty sets a debris limit, so the rules are national

mircorp.story: MirCorp was a company based in Amsterdam that tried to turn the aging Russian space station Mir into a private business. The Russian space company RSC Energia, one of its shareholders, authorised it to lease Mir for tourism, advertising, industry and science for the rest of the station's life. Its chairman was the American telecoms millionaire Walt Anderson, thought to be the main source of its first money, and its president was Jeffrey Manber. NASA's head Dan Goldin said he was not pleased, because the plan drew Russian attention and money away from the International Space Station. On 4 April 2000 MirCorp paid for the flight Soyuz TM-30, which carried Sergei Zalyotin and Aleksandr Kaleri to repair and restart the station. They were the last crew Mir ever received. The company signed up Dennis Tito as a paying passenger and said it had $100 million in future business, including a planned reality show. Its money ran out when the dot-com crash hit Anderson's investments, and US export approval arrived too late. Mir was brought down from orbit in March 2001. Tito flew to the International Space Station that year instead. Anderson later pleaded guilty to tax evasion and was sentenced to nine years in prison.
mircorp.mechanism: A private company can rent operating rights on a station registered to a country. Legal authority, launches and export licences stay with governments, and they can end the venture.
mircorp.stopped_by: Lack of money, NASA's opposition, and the deliberate destruction of Mir in March 2001
mircorp.pop: 2 cosmonauts during the Soyuz TM-30 flight in 2000
mircorp.laws: Commercial rights granted by RSC Energia on a Russian station
mircorp.challenge: Lost, as NASA pressed for Mir to be brought down and US export licences were delayed
mircorp.recognition: RSC Energia authorised it, and NASA objected
mircorp.cost: Commercial use priced at $10 million to $20 million; Manber said the company failed for lack of about $10 million

nasa-commercial-stations.story: NASA plans to replace the International Space Station with privately owned stations in low Earth orbit, where it would rent space. In December 2021, under its Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, it gave three teams a total of $415.6 million. Orbital Reef, announced by Blue Origin in October 2021 with Boeing and Sierra Space, later had its award raised to $172 million. Starlab, from Voyager Space, was raised to $217.5 million after Northrop Grumman joined it, and it later became a Voyager and Airbus venture. Axiom Space holds a separate fixed-price contract. Axiom plans to attach its first module to the existing station and then fly on its own as early as 2028. Starlab aims for 2029. A National Space Society summary says Orbital Reef remains in various stages of planning. A second funding round was meant to pick winners by April 2026, but on 28 January 2026 NASA put it on hold to match revised requirements. It issued a draft request for proposals in July 2026, and an industry report of 24 September said no award had been made. All three depend on the US government as main customer and funder. None seeks to govern itself, and none has flown.
nasa-commercial-stations.mechanism: The private successors to the space station are funded through US government agreements. Ownership moves to companies, while authorisation and control stay with a country.
nasa-commercial-stations.laws: NASA agreements and contracts, under US oversight
nasa-commercial-stations.cost: $415.6 million in first-phase NASA awards in December 2021, later raised to $172 million for Orbital Reef and $217.5 million for Starlab

orbis-lease-salter.story: The ORBIS lease is a model contract for a privately owned settlement in space, discussed in a 2019 article by Alexander Salter of Texas Tech University in the United States. The article, in the Journal of Air Law and Commerce, starts from Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which forbids any country from claiming territory in space. If that rule stays, Salter argues, the rules for human conduct in space must come from somewhere other than governments. His answer is the proprietary community, a settlement owned and run privately, whose residents accept its rules by contract. He then looks at the lease called ORBIS, drawn up by Spencer MacCallum, a scholar of such communities, and argues that this voluntary model would be expected to work better than others. Critics of private claims in space, including writers on SpaceX's terms of service, point out that Article VI still requires a country to authorise and supervise private actors in space. No settlement is known to have used the lease, and it remains a proposal on paper.
orbis-lease-salter.mechanism: The article offers contract as the source of law in space, reading the ban on national claims as leaving room for private governance. Others reply that Article VI keeps private settlers under a country's supervision.
orbis-lease-salter.laws: A model private lease in place of government law

swarm-spacebees-fcc.story: Swarm Technologies is an American satellite company founded in 2016 by Sara Spangelo and Benjamin Longmier, and it launched its first satellites without permission. In April 2017 it asked the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for an experimental licence to run four very small satellites called SpaceBEEs and two ground stations. In December 2017 the FCC refused, because it feared satellites so small could not be tracked and could become invisible debris. Swarm launched them anyway on 12 January 2018 on an Indian rocket. The launch was on foreign soil, but the FCC still had reach, because Swarm was an American company and its satellites had sent signals to ground stations in Georgia for more than a week. The agency also found unauthorised tests from weather balloons. In December 2018 Swarm signed a consent decree, a settlement enforced by the regulator. It paid a $900,000 penalty, accepted a strict compliance plan and agreed to file pre-launch reports for three years. It then made its satellites larger and easier to track, which won it a licence. SpaceX bought the company for $524 million in 2021, and its service was shut down by 2025.
swarm-spacebees-fcc.mechanism: A country's control over radio licences and ground stations gives it practical authority over satellites launched from another country.
swarm-spacebees-fcc.stopped_by: The US Federal Communications Commission, through a consent decree
swarm-spacebees-fcc.laws: The US Communications Act and FCC licensing
swarm-spacebees-fcc.challenge: Lost; it paid $900,000 and accepted oversight

vast-haven-1.story: Haven-1 is a small private space station being built in Long Beach, California, by the American company Vast, led by chief executive Max Haot. Announced in 2023, it is a single module of about 14 tons with about 45 cubic metres of living space. It depends on a docked SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule for life support and power. Crews of four would stay for up to 30 days by one account and up to two weeks by another. In early 2026 Vast moved the launch from 2026 to no earlier than the first quarter of 2027, on a Falcon 9 rocket, and Haot said in September 2026 that this date still held. Crewed flights depend on SpaceX agreeing that it is safe to dock, which Haot told Ars Technica could happen two weeks after launch or at any time in the station's three-year life. Vast's larger Haven-2 is meant to keep a crew aboard continuously after the International Space Station retires. Vast makes no claim to sovereignty. Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty requires the United States to authorise and supervise its companies in space, so a private station stays under government supervision. Haven-1 had not been launched as of November 2026.
vast-haven-1.mechanism: Under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, even a wholly private station needs its home country's authorisation and continuing supervision. Private ownership does not bring independence.
vast-haven-1.laws: None of its own, and it is expected to operate under US law

add_sources.t: Vast Maintains Early 2027 Haven-1 Launch, Aviation Week, 18 September 2026

voyager-station.story: Voyager Station was a proposed hotel in orbit, shaped like a rotating wheel, announced by the Gateway Foundation of California in 2019 under the name Von Braun Station. It would have 24 modules joined by elevator shafts and be fully working by 2027. Two years later CNN reported the new name and a builder, Orbital Assembly Corporation, run by the former pilot John Blincow, who also headed the foundation. Publicity promised regular beds, showers, bars and restaurants. Orbital Assembly's design architect Tim Alatorre said in 2019 that the eventual goal was a starship culture of people living and working in space. Reports describe it as a hotel and say nothing of separate government or legal status. Orbital Assembly was later renamed Above: Space Development Corporation, and as of 2024 it had announced no funding for its stations and had not begun construction. Its situation in 2026 is unknown, and it was not among the commercial stations named in a National Space Society summary of that year. The station has not been built.
voyager-station.mechanism: Announcing a large private settlement with no launch, licence or legal plan tests nothing in law. Publicity can run well ahead of any government authorisation.

curiosity.story: Curiosity is a car-sized NASA rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars. It landed on 6 August 2012 on the crater floor, at a spot named Bradbury Landing, to study the planet's climate and geology, and these coordinates mark that point. It has kept working well beyond its planned two years and has driven more than 36 kilometres, so its real position keeps changing. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it. So the United States keeps control of the rover wherever it goes. The ground it crosses does not become American, because Article II of the treaty bars any country from claiming land on another world.
curiosity.mechanism: Legal authority follows a spacecraft as it moves, and it stops at the machine. The ground under a rover stays unclaimed.
curiosity.why: Distance driven: the entry gave 38.16 km as of 30 October 2026, while Wikipedia gave 36.86 km as of 4 November 2026. Text now says more than 36 km, which fits both.

insight.story: InSight was a NASA lander that studied the deep interior of Mars from Elysium Planitia, a plain near the planet's equator. It landed on 26 November 2018 and confirmed marsquakes, which showed that the inside of the planet is still active. Its last contact was on 15 December 2022, and NASA declared the mission over six days later. Its seismometer and heat probe are still in place. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says a spacecraft stays under the legal authority of the country that registered it and that landing does not change who owns it. So the silent lander still belongs to the United States.
insight.mechanism: A spacecraft that has stopped working is still property. Ownership and legal authority stay with the registering country after a mission ends.

mars-3.story: Mars 3 was a Soviet probe that made the first soft landing on Mars, in the Terra Sirenum region, on 2 December 1971. It failed 110 seconds after landing, having sent only a grey image with no detail, possibly because of a huge dust storm raging at the time. The lander carried a small rover called PrOP-M, and its coordinates here are an estimate. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, was already in force. Article VIII says that landing on another world does not change who owns a spacecraft. Because Russia is the continuing state of the Soviet Union, ownership of the lander passes to Russia.
mars-3.mechanism: Ownership of a spacecraft survives both its failure and the end of the country that launched it, passing to the successor state.

mars-one.story: Mars One was a small Dutch venture that planned a permanent human colony on Mars with volunteers on a one-way trip, paid for partly by a reality television show. Its chief executive Bas Lansdorp announced it in 2012. It had two parts, a nonprofit foundation and a for-profit company, Mars One Ventures, with very few staff. It was not an aerospace firm and meant to buy rockets, spacecraft, habitats and suits from outside suppliers, at an estimated $6 billion for the first mission. Early plans sent robots first in 2020 and settlers a few years later, and by 2019 the target had slipped to 2031. The company said 202,586 people from about 140 countries applied in 2013. Joseph Roche, a physicist among the finalists, said only 2,761 had completed the process, and the company later confirmed his figure. Roche and others called it a scam, which it denied, and academics called the plan a suicide mission. Contracts for early design studies with Lockheed Martin and Surrey Satellite Technology ran out. On 15 January 2019 the Civil Court of Basel in Switzerland declared Mars One Ventures bankrupt, with debts of about 1 million euros, and an appeal failed. Lansdorp said the foundation was untouched, but the bankrupt company was the part meant to raise money. No hardware was built, and no plan for governing Mars was ever tested.
mars-one.mechanism: The one-way colony ended under ordinary Swiss bankruptcy law, long before it had to answer any question about who has legal authority on Mars.
mars-one.stopped_by: The Civil Court of Basel declared it bankrupt on 15 January 2019
mars-one.challenge: Lost in bankruptcy court, without ever reaching a space regulator
mars-one.cost: An estimated $6 billion needed; debts of about 1 million euros at bankruptcy
mars-one.why: The entry said 202,586 people applied and paid a fee. Wikipedia reports that only 2,761 completed the process, a figure the company confirmed, and 4,227 had paid by September 2013. Also changed 'founded in 2012' to 'announced in 2012'.

mars-society-city-state.story: The Mars Society is an American volunteer nonprofit, funded by donations, that lobbies for human missions to Mars. The engineer Robert Zubrin founded it on 13 August 1998 at a convention of 750 people in Boulder, Colorado. All its physical work has been on Earth. It runs analogue stations, meaning simulated Mars bases, on Devon Island in the Canadian Arctic and in the desert at its Mars Desert Research Station, where crews live under mission rules for weeks or months, including an 80-day stay in 2017. It has also asked how a society on Mars would be organised. In 2019 it held a contest to design a colony of 1,000, won by a Massachusetts Institute of Technology team with a plan called Star City, made up of five starting villages. In 2020 it announced a second contest for a city state of one million people, with a $10,000 prize. Zubrin's 2024 book The New World on Mars predicts populous Martian city-states with governments of the people that draw immigrants from Earth. The society has adopted no known constitution for Mars, and these designs have no legal force.
mars-society-city-state.mechanism: Advocates treat self-governing Martian city-states as a design problem. They have not settled how such places would fit the Outer Space Treaty, which makes countries responsible for their citizens' activities in space.
mars-society-city-state.pop: Small crews in simulated Mars stations on Earth, and nobody on Mars
mars-society-city-state.laws: Design contests and writing on Martian government, with no adopted constitution known
mars-society-city-state.cost: A $10,000 prize for the 2020 city-state contest

perseverance.story: Perseverance is a car-sized NASA rover that landed in Jezero crater on Mars on 18 February 2021, at the point marked here. The crater was chosen because its ancient river delta may hold signs of past life. The rover has been driving and collecting rock and soil samples ever since, and it has left some sealed tubes on the surface for a later mission to bring back. NASA paused its plan for that return in 2023 over its cost and turned to industry and its Jet Propulsion Laboratory for a cheaper design. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over a spacecraft and its parts. So the tubes remain under US control as they lie on Mars. The same article says ownership continues if an object returns to Earth.
perseverance.mechanism: Legal authority over a spacecraft also covers its parts, even when they are left lying apart from it. Sample tubes dropped on Mars remain under the control of the country that sent them.

phoenix.story: Phoenix was a NASA lander that came down in the Green Valley of Vastitas Borealis, in the far north of Mars, on 25 May 2008. It was the first NASA mission to land in the planet's polar region, and it went there to study water and whether the area could have supported life. It operated for 157 Martian days until the winter cut its solar power, and its last contact was on 2 November 2008. The lander is still there. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, keeps legal authority with the United States as the registering country, and landing does not change who owns the machine. The site gives the United States no claim to the polar plain.
phoenix.mechanism: Leaving a spacecraft on a plain gives no rights over the plain. The owner keeps the machine, and the land stays unclaimed.
phoenix.why: Corrected 155 sols (Martian days) to 157, per Wikipedia's Phoenix article.

starlink-mars-free-planet.story: In October 2020 SpaceX, the American rocket company, put an unusual sentence in the terms of service for the early test of its Starlink internet service. Under the section on which law applies, service on Earth or the Moon fell under California law. The next sentence read: "For Services provided on Mars, or in transit to Mars via Starship or other colonization spacecraft, the parties recognize Mars as a free planet and that no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities." Disputes there would be settled by self-governing principles agreed at the time of settlement. Because it mentions colonization spacecraft, the sentence was read as a statement about how a future colony would be run. Lawyers replied quickly. An article in Völkerrechtsblog, an international law blog, pointed to Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, under which the United States must authorise and supervise SpaceX's actions in space. It argued that SpaceX cannot opt out of this, that its conduct in space counts as that of the United States, and that such a claim risks breaching Article II, the ban on claiming land in space. A law journal note at the University of Richmond said the clause tried to sidestep international law. No one has yet reached Mars under these terms. It is not known whether the clause remains in Starlink's current terms.
starlink-mars-free-planet.mechanism: A private contract cannot release a company or its home country from Outer Space Treaty duties. The clause binds only the customer and SpaceX, and it has no effect on international law.
starlink-mars-free-planet.laws: Section 9 of the Starlink test terms said disputes on Mars would be settled by self-governing principles
starlink-mars-free-planet.challenge: Not tested in any court, and criticised by legal scholars

viking-1.story: Viking 1 was the NASA lander that became the first successful spacecraft on the surface of Mars. It touched down on the plain of Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976 and sent back the first clear image from the surface. It worked for about six years, until a faulty command from the ground ended contact on 11 November 1982. An earlier Soviet lander, Mars 3, had reached the surface in 1971 but failed within two minutes. Viking 1 still sits on the plain. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over a spacecraft and that landing does not change who owns it. So the United States still owns the machine. Neither the plain nor the planet became American.
viking-1.mechanism: Landing first gives no right to the land. The first successful lander on Mars remains US property, and the ground around it belongs to no one.

yemeni-mars-suit.story: In 1997 three men in Yemen, Adam Ismail, Mustafa Khalil and Abdullah al-Umari, filed a complaint against NASA with Yemen's Prosecutor General, accusing the American space agency of invading Mars. At the time NASA's Pathfinder mission and its small rover Sojourner were sending back more than 1,000 pictures from the planet. The men said they had inherited Mars from their ancestors 3,000 years earlier, and they based the claim on the mythologies of the Himyaritic and Sabaean civilisations of ancient Arabia. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty had already barred countries from claiming land in space. The story comes from a popular history newsletter and Wikipedia, and no court record is known. The newsletter says the chief prosecutor rejected the petition and threatened the men with jail for wasting official time. The claim came four years before Gregory Nemitz sent NASA a bill for parking on the asteroid Eros.
yemeni-mars-suit.mechanism: The men offered ancestral inheritance as a basis for owning a planet. Space law makes no allowance for this, and national courts have no authority over land on Mars.
yemeni-mars-suit.laws: Claimed inheritance from the ancient Himyaritic and Sabaean civilisations
yemeni-mars-suit.challenge: Yemen's chief prosecutor rejected the petition, according to one newsletter

zhurong.story: Tianwen-1 was China's first mission to land on another planet. Its lander set down on the plain of Utopia Planitia on Mars on 14 May 2021, making China the third country to land softly there, and the Zhurong rover rolled off eight days later. Zhurong worked for 358 days, well past its planned 93, and went into planned hibernation on 18 May 2022 ahead of sandstorms and winter. It was due to wake in December 2022 but never did, because dust covered its solar panels. Both machines remain on the surface, and sources differ slightly on the exact position. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, gives China, as the registering country, legal authority over both, and landing does not change who owns them.
zhurong.mechanism: The rule on spacecraft applies equally to every country. China holds the same rights over its Mars rover as the United States holds over its own.

apollo-11.story: Apollo 11 was the NASA mission that put the first people on the Moon, at Tranquility Base, in July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the lunar module Eagle, and its lower half, the descent stage, still stands there with an American flag, instruments and their bootprints. The coordinates are NASA's, measured from images taken by its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it, and that landing does not change who owns it. That covers the hardware only. Article II bars any country from claiming the ground beneath it, so the flag gave the United States no title to the Moon.
apollo-11.mechanism: Planting a flag gives no territory. The United States owns what it left behind, and the ground stays unclaimed.

apollo-17.story: Apollo 17 was the last crewed NASA landing on the Moon, in December 1972, in a valley called Taurus-Littrow on the southeastern rim of Mare Serenitatis. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, drove about 35.7 kilometres in a Lunar Roving Vehicle and brought back 110.52 kilograms of samples. The descent stage of their lander Challenger, the rover and a science package remain in the valley. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over its spacecraft and that landing does not change who owns them. So the United States still owns the hardware. It holds no title to the valley, because Article II bars claims to land on the Moon, and no one has landed there since.
apollo-17.mechanism: Objects left on the Moon stay the property of the country that sent them. Using a place for several days gives no rights to the land.
apollo-17.why: Entry said the astronauts covered 30 km. Wikipedia's Apollo 17 article gives about 35.7 km for the rover's total distance, so the figure was changed. The older figure could not be matched to the pages retrieved.

artemis-accords.story: The Artemis Accords are a set of non-binding principles for civil activity on the Moon and beyond, drawn up by NASA and the US State Department to go with NASA's Artemis program of Moon missions. Non-binding means no country can be taken to court for breaking them. Eight countries signed on 13 October 2020: Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States. According to NASA, Vietnam became the 78th signatory on 28 October 2026. The most debated part is the safety zone. Signatories say they will announce where they are working and coordinate so that they do not interfere with each other. A zone's size and length depend on the work done there, and it ends when the work stops. NASA says this respects the free access guaranteed by the Outer Space Treaty, which bars countries from claiming land in space. The Accords also say that extracting resources in space is possible before any further international rules exist. A McGill University paper reads this as differing from the UN Moon Agreement, which calls for an international system first. Saudi Arabia signed the Accords in July 2022 and notified its withdrawal from the Moon Agreement six months later. The China-Russia lunar base project has been described as a rival. No court has tested the zones.
artemis-accords.mechanism: A safety zone gives one operator practical priority over a place on the Moon without calling it sovereignty. This tests how far use of a place can go before it becomes the claim that the Outer Space Treaty forbids.
artemis-accords.laws: Non-binding principles agreed through arrangements between countries, covering safety zones, heritage and debris
artemis-accords.challenge: A McGill University paper says they are often seen to conflict with the Moon Agreement; no legal test has occurred

blue-ghost-1.story: Blue Ghost Mission 1 was a robotic Moon landing by Firefly Aerospace, an American private company, on a NASA-backed flight carrying ten experiments. It landed in Mare Crisium, near Mons Latreille, on 2 March 2025, and it is described as the first fully successful soft landing by a commercial company. It worked until the batteries ran down after sunset on 16 March. Because the lander belongs to a company, it shows how the law treats private hardware. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, protects its ownership and leaves legal authority with the country that registered it. Article VI makes the United States responsible for authorising and supervising its companies in space, so a private lander still answers to a government.
blue-ghost-1.mechanism: A company can own a machine on the Moon, but it remains under the supervision of its home country as Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty requires.

celestia.story: The Nation of Celestial Space, or Celestia, was a one-man claim to all of outer space by James Thomas Mangan, an American public relations man and writer from the Chicago area. He issued a declaration on 21 December 1948, and on 1 January 1949 he registered his claim with the Recorder of Deeds and Titles of Cook County, Illinois. He said he acted for humanity, to stop any one country from dominating space. The nation claimed 19 members at its foundation and 19,057 a decade later, while another source gives 100,000. In 1949 he told the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United Nations that Celestia had banned further atmospheric nuclear tests. When the space race began he sent letters of protest to the Soviet and American leaders about their flights crossing his territory, though he later waived this for satellite launches. In 1958 he applied to join the UN and raised his flag outside its New York headquarters. He issued stamps, gold and silver coins and passports, and sent passports to astronauts. No government is reported to have acted on any of this. The project is thought to have ended when he died in 1970, three years after the Outer Space Treaty barred countries from claiming space.
celestia.mechanism: A county deed office recorded the paper, but a local clerk's registration has no effect on who holds sovereignty over anything.
celestia.stopped_by: Mangan's death in 1970; nobody forced it to end
celestia.currency: Silver and gold coins called the Celeston
celestia.passports: Issued from the late 1950s, including to astronauts
celestia.challenge: Ignored by the major powers and the UN

chandrayaan-3.story: Chandrayaan-3 was an Indian Space Research Organisation mission that put the Vikram lander and the small Pragyan rover near the Moon's south pole, at about 69 degrees south, on 23 August 2023. India went there partly because studies show large amounts of ice in the region. It had lost an earlier lander, Chandrayaan-2, in 2019. The rover worked nearby for about 12 days before being put to sleep ahead of the lunar night. Both machines remain at the site, which India calls Shiv Shakti point. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, leaves legal authority over them with India as the registering country. Giving a landing point a national name has no territorial effect, because Article II bars claims to the Moon by any means.
chandrayaan-3.mechanism: A country can name the spot where it landed, but the name gives it no rights to the land.

change-4.story: Chang'e 4 was a Chinese robotic mission that made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon, on 3 January 2019, inside Von Kármán crater in the South Pole-Aitken Basin. Because the far side cannot talk directly to Earth, China first placed a relay satellite called Queqiao beyond the Moon. The lander and the Yutu-2 rover are both still on the surface. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, gives legal authority over a spacecraft to the country that registers it, which here means China. Article II bars claims to land on the Moon, so being first on the far side gives China no title to the crater.
change-4.mechanism: Reaching a place first gives no right to it under the Outer Space Treaty. China controls its machines and not the crater around them.

change-6.story: Chang'e 6 was a Chinese robotic mission that collected rock and soil from the far side of the Moon. It landed on 1 June 2024 in the southern part of Apollo Basin. Its ascent stage carried the samples back into orbit, and the return capsule reached Inner Mongolia on 25 June. The descent stage stayed behind. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, keeps legal authority over that hardware with China, and ownership continues whether an object stays on the Moon or returns to Earth. Taking samples created no claim to the site, because Article II bars any country from claiming land on the Moon.
change-6.mechanism: A country can take samples from the Moon without gaining any right to the place they came from.

for-all-moonkind.story: For All Moonkind is a nonprofit founded by Tim and Michelle Hanlon in 2017 to protect human heritage on the Moon, such as the Apollo landing sites and Neil Armstrong's bootprints. The task raises a legal problem, because the Outer Space Treaty forbids claiming the Moon, so no country can declare a protected park there as it can on its own land. The group has worked around this in several ways. In December 2018 the UN General Assembly gave it provisional observer status, which lets it speak at UN meetings on space. It helped US Senator Gary Peters draft the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act, which became law on 31 December 2020. The law applies only to companies working with NASA on lunar missions, which must agree to follow NASA guidelines that would otherwise be unenforceable. Section 9 of the Artemis Accords, signed in October 2020, also commits signatories to preserve heritage sites. In March 2021 the group released a free registry of historic lunar landing sites, and in March 2023 it formed the Institute on Space Law and Ethics. Its protections reach only those who have agreed to them.
for-all-moonkind.mechanism: Heritage on the Moon can be protected only through contracts and promises that bind those who sign them, because protecting the land itself would be a forbidden claim of territory.
for-all-moonkind.laws: The US One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (2020) and section 9 of the Artemis Accords
for-all-moonkind.recognition: Provisional observer status from the UN General Assembly, December 2018

gajardo-moon-chile.story: Jenaro Gajardo Vera, a Chilean lawyer, painter and poet, became known in his country as the legal owner of the Moon. He said that on 25 September 1954 he went before César Jiménez Fuenzalida, a notary in the city of Talca, and declared himself owner of the Moon "from before 1857". That phrase was the legal formula then used in Chile to gain ownership of land with no title deeds. He gave two reasons. One was a poetic protest, to have a say in who might live on the Moon. The other was that the Talca Social Club required members to own property. He said the deed was entered in Talca's property registry, but the registry has no record of it, and he himself gave several different dates in the 1950s. The story became public through the newspaper La Nación in October 1968. A popular tale says US President Richard Nixon asked his permission for the Apollo 11 landing, but there is no record of such a message. No authority acted on the claim, and the Outer Space Treaty barred national claims to the Moon from 1967. Gajardo died on 3 May 1998, leaving the Moon to the Chilean people in his will.
gajardo-moon-chile.mechanism: A notary can record a statement about the Moon, but national land procedures have no power over places outside the country's territory.
gajardo-moon-chile.stopped_by: His death in 1998; no authority acted
gajardo-moon-chile.laws: A notary's record using Chile's formula for land without title deeds
gajardo-moon-chile.why: Corrected: the entry said the deed was registered and gave 1954 firmly. Spanish Wikipedia says Talca's property registry has no record of the deed and that Gajardo gave other dates (1956) in interviews. Motive added. The Nixon letter is reported there as apocryphal.

ilrs.story: The International Lunar Research Station is a planned base on the Moon led by China and Russia. The two countries signed a memorandum on 9 March 2021 to build it on the surface or in lunar orbit, and their space agencies presented the plan at a conference in St Petersburg that June, describing it as open to all interested countries. Talks with European agencies in 2021 stopped after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Chinese reports in 2023 said Pakistan, the United Arab Emirates and the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization had signed agreements. Venezuela signed on 17 July 2023, which also gave China access to Venezuelan ground stations, and South Africa signed a memorandum that September. China also announced a body to coordinate the work, the International Lunar Research Station Cooperation Organization. A Xinhua report in April 2025 said 17 countries and international organisations had joined. Construction is meant to start in 2031, with a permanent base in the 2030s, and a further memorandum in May 2025 set out plans for a lunar power plant by 2036. Nothing has yet been built. It would be a state-run base under the Outer Space Treaty, which bars claims to land on the Moon.
ilrs.mechanism: Two groups of countries are now writing their own rules for Moon bases, one led by China and Russia and one by the United States. The rules on the Moon are forming through these coalitions, with no single UN system in charge.
ilrs.laws: Memoranda between partners and a planned cooperation organisation
ilrs.recognition: Agreements with partners including Venezuela, South Africa, Pakistan, the United Arab Emirates and the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization

lindsay-coles-early-deeds.story: A. Dean Lindsay of Ocilla, Georgia, was one of the first Americans to claim objects in space by paper deed. On 15 June 1936 he went to a notary in Pittsburgh and claimed all planets, islands of space and other matter visible from his home town, which he called "A.D. Lindsay's archapellago". He left out the Earth, reasoning that it belonged to its inhabitants. He first excluded the Moon and Saturn, then claimed both in separate deeds. He later explained that one May night in 1936 he had looked at the full moon, thought of it as real estate and said to himself that nobody owned it. Members of the public sent him offers to buy. He had earlier made claims on the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Mental Floss dates the recording to 28 June 1937, while Futility Closet and Wikipedia say 1936. A later seller, Robert R. Coles, a former chairman of New York's Hayden Planetarium, founded the Interplanetary Development Corporation and sold lots on the Moon for a dollar an acre. All this came about three decades before the Outer Space Treaty, and no government or court ever tested the deeds.
lindsay-coles-early-deeds.mechanism: A notary's stamp records only that a person made a statement. It gives no title, and no country's land system had authority over what was claimed.
lindsay-coles-early-deeds.laws: Quitclaim-style deeds, which pass on whatever rights a person may have, sworn before a notary
lindsay-coles-early-deeds.cost: Coles sold lots on the Moon at one dollar an acre

lonestar-lunar-data.story: Lonestar Data Holdings is a company in St Petersburg, Florida, that wants to run data centres on the Moon, and part of its pitch is legal. IEEE Spectrum, an engineering magazine, reports that over 100 countries have laws restricting where certain data may be stored, often to within their own borders, and that the company offers space as a place beyond those limits, citing the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. Its first test unit, called Freedom, flew on the Athena lander built by the American company Intuitive Machines. It carried data for the Florida state government and the Isle of Man, plus a game and a song. Athena landed on 6 March 2025 about 5 degrees from the south pole, but it came down on its side in a crater, about 250 metres or more from its target, and the mission ended after about 13 hours. Lonestar told the TV station FOX 13 that its payload was intact. The lander belonged to an American company, and under Article VI of the treaty the United States answers for its companies' activities in space. Data held there would still sit in hardware tied to a country.
lonestar-lunar-data.mechanism: Data stored on the Moon stays inside an object under the legal authority of a launching country. That runs against the idea that it would be out of reach of national law, under Articles VI and VIII of the Outer Space Treaty.
lonestar-lunar-data.laws: Marketed around national data-storage laws, citing the Outer Space Treaty
lonestar-lunar-data.recognition: Customers included the State of Florida and the Isle of Man

luna-2.story: Luna 2 was a Soviet probe launched on 12 September 1959 that crashed onto the Moon by design, the first human-made object to reach another world. Just before impact it scattered metal pennants engraved with "USSR" and the launch date. The wreckage lies near 29 degrees north, and the exact point is an estimate. The mission came before the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, and its system of registering spacecraft. Article VIII of the treaty says that being on another world does not change who owns an object, so ownership stays with Russia as the Soviet Union's continuing state. The pennants gave no claim, and Article II now bars any country from claiming the ground around them.
luna-2.mechanism: Scattering national emblems on the Moon creates no territory. The pieces remain property, and the land stays unclaimed.

luna-25.story: Luna 25 was a Russian robotic mission that crashed on the Moon. It was heading for a landing near Boguslawsky crater when, on 19 August 2023, two days before the planned landing, a failed orbit change put it on a path into the surface. It hit the inner rim of a crater, and the coordinates mark the impact, well short of the intended site. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says a spacecraft stays under the legal authority of the country that registered it and that being on another world does not change who owns it. A wreck is still an object launched into space, so the debris remains Russian property.
luna-25.mechanism: Crashing does not end ownership. Debris on the Moon stays the property of the country that launched it.

lunar-embassy.story: Lunar Embassy is a company that sells deeds to land on the Moon and other planets, run by Dennis Hope, an entrepreneur in Nevada. In 1980, going through a divorce and short of money, Hope read the Outer Space Treaty in a library. Article II bars nations from taking land in space, and Hope concluded that this left individuals free to do so. He filed a claim to the Moon, the other planets and their moons, and sent it to the United Nations with a note saying he meant to subdivide and sell it, asking them to tell him of any legal problem. Hope says they never replied, and he treats that silence as approval. He began selling full time in 1995. Discover magazine reported $9 million in sales to 4.25 million people at $19.99 an acre, and in a Vice interview he claimed 611 million lunar acres sold, plus plots on Mars, Venus, Io and Mercury.
