In 2001 customers asked about their rights, so he wrote a constitution for a Galactic Government, which he says was ratified online in March 2004 by 173,562 votes. Ram Jakhu, a space law professor at McGill University, says the treaty was written to block such claims and no one can own property in outer space. No government has ruled on the deeds, and the company's website was still selling them in 2026.
lunar-embassy.mechanism: Silence from the UN does not create ownership. Legal experts read the Outer Space Treaty's ban as blocking private claims along with national ones.
lunar-embassy.currency: A Galactic Government unit of currency is claimed
lunar-embassy.laws: A Galactic Government constitution, online from March 2004, with a claimed congress and patent office
lunar-embassy.challenge: No government has ruled on it, and Hope says the UN never replied
lunar-embassy.cost: Over $9 million in sales claimed; about $22.49 per acre in 2009; $13.3 million asked for a continent-sized parcel

lunar-registry.story: The Official Lunar Registry is a private website that sells deeds to acres on the Moon, a rival to Dennis Hope's Lunar Embassy. Its site says it has operated since 1999 with more than 125,000 customers, under a body called the International Lunar Lands Administration together with Luna Society International. Gizmodo reported in 2011 that it called itself Earth's leading lunar real-estate agency and sold land for about $20 an acre. GOOD magazine described a stated mission of funding private settlement and of living on the Moon permanently by 2015, with a moon atlas zoned for tourism, housing, science and business, and with deeds copyrighted and deposited at the US Library of Congress. No settlement followed. In 2026 the site offers lunar coordinates, certificates and ownership contracts recorded on the Ethereum blockchain, a shared digital ledger. It also lists "Lunar Republic" as a trademark, a phrase from Robert Heinlein's 1949 story The Man Who Sold the Moon. Stephen Doyle, a former NASA official quoted by Gizmodo, said people may take lunar soil but have no right to mark out a square of the surface as theirs. Who personally runs it is not stated, and no court is known to have tested its deeds.
lunar-registry.mechanism: Selling deeds to land that cannot be claimed creates a contract between buyer and seller. It transfers nothing on the Moon.
lunar-registry.laws: Deeds and certificates, now also recorded as tokens on the Ethereum blockchain
lunar-registry.cost: About $20 an acre, according to Gizmodo in 2011 and the seller's site in 2026
lunar-registry.why: Start date added from the seller's own site ('since 1999').

moon-agreement.story: The Moon Agreement is a UN treaty that treats the Moon's resources as belonging to all humanity. The UN General Assembly adopted it on 5 December 1979, and it took effect on 11 July 1984. Like the Outer Space Treaty, it says no country can claim the Moon. It goes further in Article 11, which calls the Moon's resources the common heritage of mankind and commits members to set up an international system to govern mining once mining is about to become possible. In the United States, campaigners from the L5 Society fought the treaty in 1979 and 1980, arguing that common heritage would stifle development. The United States did not join. The UN treaty database lists 17 members, including Australia, Austria, Belgium, Chile, Mexico, the Netherlands and Pakistan. France, Guatemala, India and Romania signed but never ratified, and no leading space power is a member. Saudi Arabia joined on 18 July 2012, then notified the UN on 5 January 2023 that it was leaving, about six months after it signed the US-led Artemis Accords, and its exit took effect on 5 January 2024. The treaty is in force for its members, and the international mining system has never been set up.
moon-agreement.mechanism: A treaty binds only the countries that join it. The one treaty making the Moon's resources common property has few members, and countries that want to mine have stayed out or left.
moon-agreement.laws: Article 11 calls the Moon the common heritage of mankind and requires an international system for its resources
moon-agreement.challenge: Saudi Arabia left in January 2024, and L5 Society campaigners opposed it in the United States
moon-agreement.recognition: 17 members; 11 countries signed, 7 of which went on to ratify
moon-agreement.why: Clarified the UN figure: the 11 signatories include 7 that later became members, leaving 4 that signed without ratifying.

moon-express-faa.story: Moon Express is a private American company, formed in 2010 by Robert Richards, Naveen Jain and Barney Pell, that aimed to win the Google Lunar XPRIZE contest and eventually mine the Moon. In 2016 it wanted to land its MX-1E craft, about the size of a coffee table, on the Moon. No US agency was clearly in charge of private missions beyond Earth orbit, though Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty requires a country to authorise and continually supervise its companies in space. So the company asked the Federal Aviation Administration to review the payload. On 20 July 2016 the agency gave a favorable payload determination, the first for a commercial payload meant to land on the Moon. It did so after consulting the State Department and NASA, and found no threat to safety, national security, foreign policy or treaty obligations. Lawyers at the group TechFreedom questioned whether one review letter met Article VI, and they urged Congress to pass a clear law. The mission never flew. No team in the contest was able to launch by the deadline of 31 March 2018, and the company shelved its lander plans and turned to competing for NASA delivery contracts. No report describes its activity after 2020.
moon-express-faa.mechanism: The United States met its Article VI duty for this lunar mission through an improvised review by an aviation regulator, because no dedicated law existed.
moon-express-faa.laws: A Federal Aviation Administration payload approval, with reference to Articles IV and VI of the Outer Space Treaty
moon-express-faa.challenge: No challenge; approved after review by several agencies
moon-express-faa.recognition: US government approval of one mission

shackleton-south-pole.story: Shackleton is a crater almost exactly at the Moon's south pole, and it marks the region that the United States and China both want to reach. The attraction is water ice thought to lie in nearby permanently dark areas, which could support human outposts or make rocket fuel. NASA named nine candidate landing regions around the pole in October 2024. In 2026 it changed its plan, so that Artemis III became a test in Earth orbit in 2027 and crews would land on Artemis IV and V in 2028, with the pole still the destination. China's Chang'e 7 is planned to land on Shackleton's rim to search for ice and scout a site for the International Lunar Research Station, the base China and Russia announced in 2021. The craft reached its launch pad in August 2026, but the launch was postponed and is now expected in 2027. Nothing has landed at this site, so no spacecraft is yet under Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty there. Article II bars any country from claiming the ground.
shackleton-south-pole.mechanism: No country can own the lunar south pole, however useful its ice. Whoever arrives first gets control of their own machines and no rights over the land.
shackleton-south-pole.why: Updated for 2026: Artemis III is no longer a Moon landing, and Chang'e 7 was postponed after rollout (Wikipedia now says 2027). Also set built to false, because the entry marks a target area where nothing has landed.

add_sources.t: NASA is Full Steam Ahead on Artemis III, IV and V, SpacePolicyOnline, 23 October 2026
China Postponed Its Chang'e 7 Lunar Mission, The Diplomat, September 2026

slim.story: SLIM, the Smart Lander for Investigating Moon, was a Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission to prove that a craft could land within about 100 metres of its target. It touched down near Shioli crater on 19 January 2024, making Japan the fifth country to land softly on the Moon. It came down on its side with its solar panels facing away from the Sun, so it was shut down within hours and woke only when the light changed. It survived three lunar nights, with its last contact in April 2024, and JAXA ended the mission that August. The silent spacecraft remains Japanese property. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, keeps legal authority with the registering country and sets no end date tied to the life of a mission.
slim.mechanism: Legal authority over a spacecraft does not end when the mission does. A dead lander stays under the country that registered it.

unreal-estate-pop.story: Virgiliu Pop is a Romanian space lawyer, born in 1974, who wrote the main history of private claims to the Moon. His doctoral thesis at the University of Glasgow in Scotland was on rights to land in outer space. His book Unreal Estate: The Men Who Sold the Moon, reviewed in The Space Review in 2006, traces claims back 250 years to Prussia, where a king was said to have granted the Moon to a farmer with healing powers. That story surfaced only in the 1990s, when a descendant, Martin Juergens of Germany, contested Dennis Hope's claims. Wikipedia gives the date as 15 July 1756 and the king as Frederick the Great. Pop sorts claimants into groups, including those selling acres for money, and in his final chapter he takes apart the legal argument of Hope's Lunar Embassy. He says such claims are a trivial issue for space lawyers, yet they have shaped the public's view of space law, and he reported that several million people held such certificates. To make his point he himself claimed ownership of the Sun, a claim he says is as bogus as the others.
unreal-estate-pop.mechanism: Pop argues that the Outer Space Treaty closes off private land claims in space. His mock claim on the Sun shows that anyone can produce such a paper.
unreal-estate-pop.recognition: Member of the International Institute of Space Law

fonuafoou-falcon-island.story: Fonuafoʻou, meaning "new land" in Tongan, is an undersea volcano in the western Haʻapai islands of Tonga that has built an island several times. The crew of the British ship HMS Falcon spotted the site in 1867, when it was a coral reef. On 11 October 1885 the volcano erupted, and three days later an island stood there, which the British named Falcon Island. Eruptions in 1894, 1921, 1927, 1928, 1933 and 1936 kept building it up, and by 1949 it was reported at 6 kilometres across and 145 metres high. That year another eruption blew the island apart and it collapsed under the sea. There were further eruptions in 1970 and 1993, and the top now lies 17 metres below the surface. The island existed on and off for about 64 years and carried both a British and a Tongan name, and nothing stands above the water today.
fonuafoou-falcon-island.mechanism: Volcanic land can appear and vanish at the same spot. Under Article 121 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a place counts as an island only while it stays above water at high tide.

graham-island-ferdinandea.story: Graham Island was a volcanic island that rose from the Mediterranean Sea about 30 kilometres south of Sicily in July 1831 and sank again within six months. By 17 July a Sicilian customs official, Michele Fiorini, had landed and planted an oar to claim it for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, the state then ruling southern Italy. On 2 August Captain Humphrey Senhouse of the Royal Navy claimed it for Britain and named it after Sir James Graham, head of the Admiralty, because the navy thought it could help control Mediterranean shipping. King Ferdinand II sent the warship Etna and called it Ferdinandea. The French geologist Constant Prévost named it Julia, and Spain also declared an interest. At its largest it was about 4 square kilometres and 63 metres high, with two small lakes, and tourists came to see it. It was made of loose volcanic ash, which waves wore down, and officials reported no trace of it by 17 December. The dispute lapsed unsettled. Its summit now lies about 6 metres under water. When it showed signs of activity in 2000 and 2002, Italians placed a flag and a marble plaque on the bank to head off future claims.
graham-island-ferdinandea.mechanism: New land in the sea can attract rival claims within weeks. These four were never settled, because the island wore away after about six months and left nothing to decide.
graham-island-ferdinandea.stopped_by: Waves eroded the loose ash, and the island disappeared
graham-island-ferdinandea.recognition: The rival claims were never settled
